prompt.context: Hugo Noos (HN) is a premier apparel brand that produces clothes and shoes for men and women of all ages. It has two product lines: Regular (less pricy, more casual, younger consumers) and Premium (higher priced, business attire). HN currently sells through large premium retail stores such as Macy's and Nordstrom as well as through its own retail stores. The company does not currently sell items online. The industry is stable, and the company has sufficient human, financial, and other resources to expand. Focus only on the US market. Current annual profit is $1B.
prompt.question: Hugo Noos wants to increase profits by opening an online sales channel, targeting a 20% profit increase. The CEO has asked us to determine whether this is feasible and how the company should proceed.

clarifying_info.q: Do the retail stores currently sell online?
clarifying_info.a: No, assume retail stores do not currently sell items online.

clarifying_info.q: What are the retail prices for each product line?
clarifying_info.a: Retail price of a regular item is $240 and retail price of a premium item is $345.

clarifying_info.q: What discount will HN offer online?
clarifying_info.a: The client is considering decreasing prices 20% for regular items and 15% for premium items for the own-platform option.

clarifying_info.q: How many units can HN sell online per day?
clarifying_info.a: For the own platform: Regular 5,500 SKU/day; Premium 2,500 SKU/day. Assume 350 operating days per year.

clarifying_info.q: What are the variable costs per item?

framework: Identify the three channel options: (1) own online platform, (2) leverage existing retailer platforms (Macy's/Nordstrom online), (3) use third-party marketplace platforms such as Amazon
For each channel option, assess revenue impact (pricing, volume), cost structure (fixed and variable), cannibalization of existing brick-and-mortar sales, and strategic/brand considerations
Compare profitability of each option against the $200M target (20% of $1B)
Identify strategic pros and cons beyond the numbers (brand control, data access, flexibility)
Recommend a path with mitigating actions to address key risks

questions.prompt: Step 1 – Own Platform: Calculate the annual profit from launching HN's own online platform, then assess whether it meets the 20% profit increase target.
questions.guidance: Candidate should build a P&L: compute revenue from both lines, identify fixed costs (platform investment amortized or listed as annual service costs), variable costs including delivery and packaging, and factor in cannibalization. Should note that a 20% price discount on premium items risks brand dilution and cannibalization, and probe whether premium items need to match retail price.

math.setup: Revenue: Regular 5,500 SKU/day × $200 (240×0.8) × 350 days + Premium 2,500 SKU/day × $300 (345×~0.87≈$293, rounded to $300 per casebook) × 350 days. Fixed costs: Annual service $25M, Insurance $3M, Wages $15M, Incremental warehouse $25M, Marketing $50M. Variable costs: (Regular 5,500 + Premium 2,500) × 350 days × ($80 or $85 + $10 + $13). Cannibalization: store profit drops 20% = $200M loss.
steps: Regular variable cost per SKU: $80 + $10 + $3 = $93; Premium: $85 + $10 + $3 = $98
Variable cost Regular: 5,500 × $93 × 350 = $178.9M; Premium: 2,500 × $98 × 350 = $85.75M; Total variable ≈ $256M (per casebook, combined ~$256M, total all costs ~$388M per casebook rounding)
math.answer: Online platform profit = ~$259M; after $200M cannibalization loss, net profit increase is ~$59M. Total company profit rises to ~$1.059B, a ~5.9% increase — well short of the 20% target on a standalone basis.

questions.prompt: Step 2 – Third-Party Platform Partnership: How does revenue and cost structure change if HN sells through an existing platform (e.g., Amazon)? Calculate profit under this scenario.
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize: higher volume due to larger user base, lower fixed costs (no site build) but platform fee, potentially lower marketing spend. Should think about pricing leverage and whether HN can maintain price parity. Should compute revenue and costs using the partnership assumptions.

math.setup: Regular: 7,000 SKU/day × $200 × 350 days. Premium: 2,500 SKU/day × $345 × 350 days (no discount for premium). Fixed costs: Platform fee $50M, Insurance $3M, Wages $5M, Warehouse $30M, Marketing $20M. Variable costs same per SKU.
steps: Variable cost Regular: 7,000 × $93 × 350 = $227.85M; Premium: 2,500 × $98 × 350 = $85.75M; Total ≈ $313M (per casebook ~$313M)
math.answer: Partnership channel generates ~$370M profit before cannibalization — exceeding the $200M target even if some cannibalization occurs. This option outperforms the own-platform scenario on raw profit.

questions.prompt: Step 3 – Strategic Pros and Cons: What are the strategic benefits and risks of running an own website versus using an existing platform?
questions.guidance: Candidate should go beyond the math and address brand, data, control, and scale dimensions for each option.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the strategic benefits of running HN's own platform versus partnering with an existing platform like Amazon or using retailer online channels?

categories.name: Own Platform – Benefits
ideas: Strategic control over the sales channel — full transparency of shelf placement and inventory
Ability to feature complementary products from other brands as an additional revenue stream
Complete control of marketing and brand presentation, reducing risk of brand deterioration
Greater pricing flexibility without third-party fee structures
Richer first-party customer data for targeted marketing

categories.name: Own Platform – Risks
ideas: High upfront and ongoing investment ($5M build + $25M annual service)
Lower initial traffic and consumer base compared to established platforms
Greater operational complexity (warehousing, fulfillment, customer service)
Potentially negative NPV if volume ramp-up is slow

categories.name: Third-Party Platform – Benefits
ideas: Access to a large existing consumer base, driving higher volume
Platform provides database tools for better inventory management and marketing campaigns
Faster time-to-market — no site development lead time
Better sales forecasting through platform analytics

categories.name: Third-Party Platform – Risks
ideas: Brand deterioration risk if placed alongside lower-tier brands
Higher cannibalization potential from broader consumer exposure
Less control over pricing, promotions, and positioning
Dependency on third-party platform terms and fee structures
Loss of direct customer relationship and first-party data

recommendation: If pursuing own platform: sell premium products at the same price as retail stores and discount only the regular line; create some online-exclusive items to reduce cannibalization; explore partnerships with complementary apparel brands to carry supplementary products on the HN site

If pursuing partnership: negotiate contract terms to maintain price control and prevent cannibalization; require a sales data-sharing agreement to strengthen inventory and demand forecasting; ensure brand presentation standards are contractually enforced

Partnership likely delivers higher near-term profit ($370M vs $59M net), while own platform offers greater long-term brand and strategic control — final recommendation depends on HN's strategic priorities
risks: Own platform: negative NPV risk if volume targets are not achieved; ongoing fixed cost burden
Partnership: brand dilution and higher cannibalization; loss of pricing and channel control
Both paths: cannibalization of existing $1B profit base if pricing and channel strategy is not managed carefully
next_steps: Conduct NPV analysis on own platform investment factoring in multi-year volume ramp
Negotiate pilot partnership terms with one platform to test volume and cannibalization impact
Define online-exclusive SKUs to protect brick-and-mortar demand
Establish clear KPIs for brand health (price index, search rank, return rates) before full launch
